note: The English Lordship of Ireland (1171–) was established when Henry II invaded to bring the Norman barons who had conquered Leinster (under Strongbow/Richard de Clare) under royal control. Pope Alexander III endorsed the invasion through the bull Laudabiliter (c. 1155, authenticity disputed). The subsequent English presence was limited: the 'Pale' around Dublin controlled by the crown; the 'Land of Peace' governed by Anglo-Norman lords who gradually 'went native'; and the 'Land of War' of Gaelic chiefs who accepted nominal English suzerainty. Ireland was never fully conquered in the medieval period.

_quarry.structural_significance: The English lordship creates the pattern of partial conquest and cultural assimilation ('going native') that defines Anglo-Irish relations; the failure to complete the conquest leaves a permanently contested frontier; the contrast between Pale and Gaelic Ireland prefigures modern Northern Ireland
